newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan set for new financial inspection body.
newsitem.headline: Japan set for new financial inspection body.

text.p: Japan's Lower House of parliament on Thursday cleared the way to set up a new government agency to police the country's scandal-hit financial sector.

There was little opposition to a bill setting up the agency under the Prime Minister's Office to inspect and supervise financial institutions, functions carried out in the past by the powerful Ministry of Finance (MOF).

MOF, long viewed as Japan's elite ministry, has come under fire for failing to uncover recent scandals involving dubious dealings with racketeers by a leading Japanese bank Dai-ichi Kangyo Bank and top brokerage firm Nomura Securities Co Ltd.
Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto last week lashed out at both DKB and the finance ministry over the scandal.
"It's not only a matter of DKB," he told reporters. "There must have been inspections by the MOF."

In 1991, Hashimoto himself was forced to resign as finance minister over a scandal at Nomura and other brokerages over compensation of favoured clients and ties to organised crime, as well as loan fraud scams at some of the nation's top banks.
The ministry has also been criticised for its handling of Japan's bad loans crisis, mostly for the secretive manner in which it has dealt with the individual crises.
Public outrage flared last year over the budgeting of 685 billion yen ($5.90 billion) to help liquidate failed "jusen" mortgage firms.
The new agency starts operations in July after parliament's rubber stamp Upper House passes the bill.
Some analysts, while applauding the move, wondered if it would get the resources needed to check on banks and brokerages, any better than MOF has done.

"The new watchdog body must be given the people and electronic monitoring systems needed, but I haven't seen anything to suggest they will be given the resources to do their job properly," said Brian Waterhouse, financial analyst at HSBC James Capel.
In a bid to get its finances under control, the government is considering a recommendation that there should be a cap on overall government staff costs until 2003.
DKB has said it provided a cumulative total of 26 billion yen ($224 million) in loans to a company linked to a corporate racketeer, and may have concealed details of the loan before MOF inspections.
"I'm sure they (MOF) should have found it (DKB's dubious loans), but you have to have the resources. The inspection team is probably pretty capable, but it is extremely stretched." ($1=116)
